## Introduction

The Inference pages share one **known-truth** case study. We pick parameter
values, simulate *pseudo-observed* data there, and check whether a method
recovers them. Run this kind of recovery test before pointing a method at field
data.

This page builds the case study and covers the first of the three steps in
@hartig2011: **aggregation**, the choice of summary statistics. It ends with
everything a method page needs: the pseudo-observed data, 200 simulations from
the prior, and the scale of each statistic. Method pages start from the middle
with one call, `case.load(...)`, which reuses the runs this page made.

::: {.callout-note}
## Runtime

The first render runs about 250 simulations of a small model (roughly 15
minutes on a laptop, one simulation at a time). They are stored in the shared
registry `forevertree.duckdb`, so later pages reuse them instead of
re-simulating.
:::

The case study's code lives in one module,
`examples/sbi_forevertree/forevertree_case.py`. The docs pages and the
command-line example `run_abc.py` both import it:

```{python}
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, "../../examples/sbi_forevertree")
import forevertree_case as case
import pandas as pd

from joshpy.cli import JoshCLI
from joshpy.jar import JarMode
from joshpy.registry import RunRegistry

registry = RunRegistry("forevertree.duckdb")  # shared by the Inference pages
cli = JoshCLI(josh_jar=JarMode.DEV)
```

## The Model

We use the ForeverTree model from the Josh paper: ten trees per 16 km cell, on
a grid of 63 cells, grow each year by up to `maxNewGrowth`, scaled by a
temperature response and a precipitation response. Drought slows growth, and
`minPrecipImpactPct` sets how much: at 0% a dry year halts growth, at 100%
drought has no effect.

The model is **stochastic**: each tree's growth each year is multiplied by a
draw from a normal distribution with mean 100% and standard deviation 5%. Each
run is therefore one draw from a distribution of outputs,
$p(D_\text{sim} \mid \theta)$, that we can sample but can't write down. That is
why the likelihood is intractable and has to be approximated
[@hartig2011, fig. 2].

| Parameter | Meaning | Prior | Truth |
|-----------|---------|-------|-------|
| `maxNewGrowth` | Maximum height gain per year | Uniform, 0.2 to 2.0 m | 1.0 m |
| `minPrecipImpactPct` | Growth retained in the driest years | Uniform, 0 to 100% | 40% |

## Put `{run_hash}` in the export path

`SbiStrategy` runs each batch of parameter sets **before** loading any of them,
so every run needs its own output file:

```josh
exportFiles.patch = "file:///tmp/forevertree_abc_{run_hash}_{replicate}.csv"
```

Without `{run_hash}` (or `{label}`), every run in a batch would write the same
CSV, so joshpy refuses such a batch with an error.
:::

## The Pseudo-Observed Data: a Survey

Field data are never as complete as a simulation's output. A monitoring program
measures a fixed set of sites, each with error. To mirror that, the
pseudo-observed data are a **survey**:

- the final-year mean tree height of **8 fixed cells**, spread across the
  climate gradient;
- each **measured with error**: normal, with a standard deviation of
  0.25 m.

The same survey is applied to the truth and to every simulation. Statistics
must be computed the same way for observed and simulated data, and simulating
the survey makes its error part of the variability that comes from within the
model. The tolerance $\varepsilon$ then carries only the approximation error.
The alternative is to leave the survey unsimulated and size $\varepsilon$ to the
observation error, which makes ABC exact for the model plus that error model
[@wilkinson2013].

The survey, from raw output to measured heights:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
case.show_source(case.final_heights, case.measurement_rng, case.survey)
```

The measurement noise is seeded from the run and replicate, so a run that is
reused or replayed is measured exactly as before.

The truth run gets its own seed (`seed=1`), so the page is reproducible. The
simulations used for inference leave `seed` unset, so each draws its own noise,
as independent realizations of a stochastic model should.

```{python}
truth_job, observed = case.observe_truth(registry, cli)
truth_survey = case.survey(registry, truth_job.run_hash)
truth_survey.round(2)
```

## Simulating the Prior

Every ABC method starts by simulating parameter sets drawn from the prior. We
draw 200 with sbi's rejection ABC (`method="mcabc"`) set to keep every draw
(`quantile=1.0`), which makes it a plain prior simulation:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
case.show_source(case.simulate_prior)
```

```{python}
prior = case.simulate_prior(registry, cli, observed)
reference = case.reference_table(registry, [job for job, _ in prior.job_results])
reference.drop(columns="run_hash").describe().loc[["count", "mean", "std", "min", "max"]].round(3)
```

Each row of `reference` holds one simulation's parameters and its candidate
statistics: the **reference table** of ABC [@csillery2012]. The registry holds
every run's full output, so statistics we haven't thought of yet can be
computed later without re-simulating.

## Choosing Summary Statistics

A summary statistic must change with the parameters, and it must be computed
the same way for observed and simulated data. From the survey, four candidates
come to mind:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
case.show_source(case.statistics)
```

Plotting each candidate against each parameter, over the prior simulations,
shows what each one can tell us. The dashed line is the pseudo-observed value
and the dotted line the true parameter; ρ is the Spearman rank correlation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-candidates
#| fig-cap: "Candidate statistics of the survey against each parameter, over 200 prior simulations. The mean moves with both parameters; the CV moves with drought sensitivity (minPrecipImpactPct) and hardly at all with growth."
case.plot_candidates(reference, case.statistics(truth_survey["measured"]))
```

```{python}
statistic_names = list(case.LABELS)
correlations = reference[list(case.PRIOR) + statistic_names].corr(method="spearman")
correlations.loc[statistic_names, list(case.PRIOR)].rename(index=case.LABELS).round(2)
```

**Why the CV and not the variance?** The pair (mean, variance) and the pair
(mean, CV) carry the same information: each can be computed from the other, so
neither is more sufficient. What differs is how the distance combines them,
and that matters because the tolerance is not zero.

ForeverTree is multiplicative in `maxNewGrowth`:

```josh
newGrowth.step = meta.maxNewGrowth * temperatureImpact * precipImpact * stochastic
```

So every cell's height scales with `maxNewGrowth`. The mean and the SD of the
surveyed heights scale with it, and the variance with its square. The CV
(SD / mean) cancels it and tracks drought sensitivity, which spreads wet and dry
cells apart. A little dependence on growth remains, because the measurement
error is additive and weighs more when trees are short.

So **mean + CV gives roughly one statistic per parameter**: the CV pins down
`minPrecipImpactPct`, and the mean then pins down `maxNewGrowth`. Mean + variance
mixes both parameters in both statistics, and the variance's prior spread is
dominated by the fastest-growing draws, which leaves it little resolution near
the truth.

**Are these statistics sufficient?** A statistic is *sufficient* if it keeps all
the information in the data that is relevant to the parameters. Then
$p(\theta \mid S_\text{obs}) = p(\theta \mid D_\text{obs})$. Minimal sufficiency
is desirable but not required [@hartig2011]. We don't know whether mean and CV
are sufficient: the figure shows they are *informative*, which is weaker. The
survey also discards most cells and the whole height trajectory before the
final year. Sufficiency usually has to be tested on artificial data
[@hartig2011]; the SMC-ABC page does that by dropping the CV.

Pattern-oriented modelling makes the same point in ecological terms: its
"patterns" are summary statistics, and combining patterns observed at different
scales is a recognized way to approach sufficiency [@grimm2005; @hartig2011].

## Scaling

Most ABC methods compare statistics with a Euclidean distance, which adds up the
differences in each statistic, so a statistic with a larger spread would
dominate. Following @hartig2011, who cite @beaumont2002, we divide each
statistic by its standard deviation across the prior simulations:

```{python}
scale = {name: float(reference[name].std()) for name in case.STATISTICS}
study = case.CaseStudy(truth_job, truth_survey, reference, scale)

pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "pseudo-observed": study.observed,
        "prior SD (scale)": scale,
        "pseudo-observed (prior SDs)": study.observed_scaled,
    }
).rename(index=case.LABELS).round(3)
```

## From Model Output to a Comparison

Here is the whole aggregation step for the truth run, ending in the comparison
an ABC method makes. For illustration, the tolerance $\varepsilon$ is set so
that the closest 10% of the prior simulations fall within it, which is
rejection ABC at a 10% acceptance rate.

```{python}
epsilon = float(study.distance(reference).quantile(0.1))
print(f"ε = {epsilon:.3f} prior SDs")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-pipeline
#| fig-cap: "From model output to a comparison, for the pseudo-observed run. (1) Final-year height of all 63 cells; outlined cells are surveyed. (2) The survey measures each with error. (3) The measured heights reduce to a mean and a CV. (4) In units of prior SDs, the pseudo-observed statistics are compared with each prior simulation's; those within ε (dashed circle) are accepted."
case.plot_pipeline(study, registry, epsilon)
```

## What the Likelihood Approximation Compares

At a single $\theta$, ABC's likelihood approximation asks how often a
simulation lands within $\varepsilon$ of $S_\text{obs}$. To see what that
involves, we run 50 replicates at the truth, as one job with its own seed
(`seed=2`), and survey each one twice: once without measurement error (model
noise only) and once with it.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
case.show_source(case.replicate_study)
```

```{python}
replicates = case.replicate_study(registry, cli, n=50)
replicates["distance"] = study.distance(replicates)

spread = replicates.groupby("observation")[case.STATISTICS].std() / pd.Series(scale)
spread.rename(columns=case.LABELS).round(4)
```

```{python}
replicates.groupby("observation")["distance"].describe()[["50%", "max"]].round(4)
```

The first table gives each statistic's spread between replicates, in prior SDs;
the second, how far the replicates land from $S_\text{obs}$.

```{python}
#| label: fig-replicates
#| fig-cap: "Fifty replicate simulations at the true parameters, surveyed without (model only) and with measurement error, in units of each statistic's prior SD. Left and centre: offsets from the pseudo-observed statistics (dashed), which are themselves one draw with measurement error. Right: the fraction of replicates within ε of the pseudo-observed statistics, the indicator-kernel estimate of the ABC likelihood at the truth, against ε; the dashed line marks the 10% rejection tolerance."
case.plot_replicates(study, replicates, epsilon)
```

The fraction of replicates within $\varepsilon$ estimates the ABC likelihood at
the truth for that tolerance (an indicator kernel). An ABC method estimates it
implicitly at every $\theta$ it proposes, with one simulation each.

Two things follow from the figure:

- **The survey's measurement error is the larger noise source.** Model noise
  averages out over the 10 trees in each cell, so it barely moves the survey
  statistics; the measurement error on 8 cells moves them much more. The
  pseudo-observed data are one draw from the orange distributions, not their
  centre.
- **The tolerance decides what the posterior's width means.** Where
  $\varepsilon$ is far above the replicate distances, every replicate counts as
  a match, the likelihood at the truth is close to 1, and the posterior's width
  reflects the tolerance rather than the data's noise. The width starts to
  reflect the survey's noise only once a search tightens $\varepsilon$ toward
  the replicate distances, which is what the SMC-ABC page's simulation budget
  has to buy.

## Starting a Method Page

Everything above is stored in the registry. A method page starts from the
middle with one call, which reuses these runs instead of re-simulating:

```{python}
#| eval: false
import forevertree_case as case

study = case.load(registry, cli)  # pseudo-observed survey, prior simulations, scale
summaries, observed = study.abc_target()  # scaled summaries function and S_obs, for SbiStrategy
```

```{python}
registry.close()  # the registry stays on disk for the other Inference pages
```
